teach: From the lesson: empresa comes from an old word for an undertaking — the thing a man takes on with both hands.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La empresa — the company, the business as a whole, the thing you built.' Another way to hold it: empresa comes from an old word for an undertaking — the thing a man takes on with both hands
walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen opens with the biggest word of the day, the house everything else lives in. (2) That word is la empresa. (3) It means: the company.

teach: From the lesson: if empresa is the house, negocio is the work that happens inside the house — the business in motion.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'El negocio — the business, the deal, the work of making a living. El negocio.' Another way to hold it: if empresa is the house, negocio is the work that happens inside the house — the business in motion
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson gives two big words: empresa for the company as a whole. (2) Its everyday brother is el negocio. (3) Negocio means: the business.

teach: From the lesson: clientes and clients are cousins — the same word wearing Spanish clothes — and they are Bill's people at work.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Los clientes — the clients, the customers, the people who trust you with their money and their name.' Another way to hold it: clientes and clients are cousins — the same word wearing Spanish clothes — and they are Bill's people at work
walk: Walk it through: (1) A company is people, and the lesson names the people on the other side of the desk. (2) Their word sounds almost like its English cousin. (3) Los clientes means: the clients.

teach: From the lesson: trabajo is a word with sweat in it — the labor, the job, the whole working life.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'El trabajo — the work, the job. El trabajo. Say it: El trabajo. Trabajo is a word with sweat in it — in the old language underneath Spanish, its root carried the idea of effort, of something that costs you something.' Another way to hold it: trabajo is a word with sweat in it — the labor, the job, the whole working life
walk: Walk it through: (1) Clientes and the company do something together: they work. (2) The word for that work itself is el trabajo. (3) It means: the work.

q: Which phrase means 'I have a call'?
teach: From the lesson: tengo is I have, from lesson three, and llamada is a call — llamar, to call, wearing a noun's clothes.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tengo una llamada — I have a call, I have a phone call. Tengo una llamada.' Another way to hold it: tengo is I have, from lesson three, and llamada is a call — llamar, to call, wearing a noun's clothes
walk: Walk it through: (1) Tengo means I have — tengo dinero, I have money. (2) A call is una llamada. (3) Joined, I have a call is: Tengo una llamada.

teach: From the lesson: reunión is built from unir, to unite — a bringing-together-again of people with work to do.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Una reunión means a meeting — a gathering, a coming-together; reunión is built from unir, to unite, to bring together, with re- in front of it: a bringing-together-again.' Another way to hold it: reunión is built from unir, to unite — a bringing-together-again of people with work to do
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson names the event that fills a businessman's calendar. (2) It is built on the idea of people coming together. (3) Una reunión means: a meeting.

teach: From the lesson: computadora names the machine by what it does — the machine that computes — and it is where el correo lives.
teach2: From the lesson: 'La computadora — the computer. La computadora. Say it: La computadora. Computadora, the machine that computes — longer than the English word, more honest too; it names the machine by what it does.' From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La computadora — the computer. La computadora. Say it: La computadora.' Another way to hold it: computadora names the machine by what it does — the machine that computes — and it is where el correo lives
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson names the desk piece by piece: oficina, teléfono, correo. (2) The machine among them is la computadora. (3) It means: the computer.

q: Carmen teaches the -ar verbs by feel: trabajar is 'to work.' What is 'I work'?
teach: From the lesson: the -ar ending steps aside and the verb signs with -o — and the o means I.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Trabajar, to work, becomes: Trabajo — I work. Trabajo. Say it with me, and stand up a little straighter when you say it, because it is a working man's sentence in one word: Trabajo.' Another way to hold it: the -ar ending steps aside and the verb signs with -o — and the o means I
walk: Walk it through: (1) Trabajar is the full form, to work. (2) When Bill himself does the action, Carmen changes the ending to -o. (3) So I work is: Trabajo.

q: What does 'Hablo con los clientes' mean?
teach: From the lesson: hablo is I speak — hablar wearing the -o — and con means with.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Hablo con los clientes — I speak with the clients. Con means with. Hablo con los clientes.' Another way to hold it: hablo is I speak — hablar wearing the -o — and con means with
walk: Walk it through: (1) Hablo is the I form of hablar, to speak. (2) Con means with, and los clientes are the clients. (3) Whole: I speak with the clients.

teach: From the lesson: vender is to sell, from the second verb family, and vendo is the I form a businessman needs at a desk.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Vendo — I sell. Vendo. Say it: Vendo. Hear the difference in the ending: the -ar family signs with -o after dropping -ar — trabajo — and vender signs vendo, I sell.' Another way to hold it: vender is to sell, from the second verb family, and vendo is the I form a businessman needs at a desk
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson introduces vender, to sell. (2) Its I form is the seller's statement. (3) Vendo means: I sell.

q: Which sentence does Carmen teach for naming Bill's assistant, Dave?
teach: From the lesson: ayudante is the assistant, the helper — and se llama is the same naming shape that names Bill, Jillian, and the empresa.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mi ayudante se llama Dave — my assistant is called Dave, my helper's name is Dave.' Another way to hold it: ayudante is the assistant, the helper — and se llama is the same naming shape that names Bill, Jillian, and the empresa
walk: Walk it through: (1) Ayudante means assistant or helper. (2) Se llama is the naming shape from lesson one. (3) The sentence is: Mi ayudante se llama Dave.

q: In your own words: what happens to a verb like 'trabajar' when Bill is the one doing the action, and what does the new ending say?
teach: From the lesson: the verb puts on the o, and the o is Bill's signature on the verb — it says: I am the one doing this.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'In Spanish, when a verb's full form ends in -ar, the I form ends in -o — and you do not need to recite that rule to anyone, ever.' Another way to hold it: the verb puts on the o, and the o is Bill's signature on the verb — it says: I am the one doing this
walk: Walk it through: (1) Trabajar, hablar, llamar, comprar all end in -ar. (2) Carmen changes the ending for the I form. (3) The new ending is -o, and it means I: trabajo, hablo, llamo, compro.
